steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
People have been investigating and measuring eye movement trajectories since the beginning of the twentieth century. Since then they have been used for a long time in many areas of psychology, cognitive science and applied research. But over this long history, the number of methods to quantitatively describe eye movement trajectories did not change as much as the number of scientific works that use eye tracking. Most quantitative measures are statistics of macro events, where every eye movement trajectory is split into saccades and fixations. Finding saccades in eye tracker data is strongly connected to calculating velocities, usually with a very simple two-point central difference approach. The easiest way is the simple difference from sample to sample. But this makes the noise in the signal much bigger. So all this means that descriptive statistics based on macro events depend on which algorithm was chosen to approximate velocity, and in most cases they are extremely unstable to noise in the signal. So new properties that describe the whole eye movement trajectory holistically extract quantitative features from the whole trajectory. Because these features are holistic, topological features persist with any kind of random noise in the signal.

A vast and distributed neural system controls eye movement trajectories, so they are affected by mental and neurological disorders such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Parkinson’s disease. So looking for new features of eye movement trajectories could help with diagnosing mental and neurological disorders. Other areas that could benefit from better features are ophthalmology and medical decision-making, where eye movement trajectory data removes potential sources of error in image-based diagnostics.

- Data collection
  - infrared light into viewer's eyes; reflection from cornea (transparent front part covering pupil)
  - gaze point from relative positions of pupil and corneal reflection
  - basic form: time series of x and y in pixels relative to screen resolution
  - extras depending on tracker and experiment: pupil diameter, direction vector
- This work
  - investigated different topological features of human eye movement trajectories
  - compared with specific macro-event statistics on a classification problem

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
People have been investigating and measuring eye movement trajectories since the beginning of the twentieth century. Since then they have been used for a long time in many areas of psychology, cognitive science and applied research. But over this long history, the number of methods to quantitatively describe eye movement trajectories did not change as much as the number of scientific works that use eye tracking. Most quantitative measures are statistics of macro events, where every eye movement trajectory is split into saccades and fixations. Finding saccades in eye tracker data is strongly connected to calculating velocities, usually with a very simple two-point central difference approach. The easiest way is the simple difference from sample to sample. But this makes the noise in the signal much bigger. So all this means that descriptive statistics based on macro events depend on which algorithm was chosen to approximate velocity, and in most cases they are extremely unstable to noise in the signal. So new properties that describe the whole eye movement trajectory holistically extract quantitative features from the whole trajectory. Because these features are holistic, topological features persist with any kind of random noise in the signal.

A vast and distributed neural system controls eye movement trajectories, so they are affected by mental and neurological disorders such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Parkinson’s disease. So looking for new features of eye movement trajectories could help with diagnosing mental and neurological disorders. Other areas that could benefit from better features are ophthalmology and medical decision-making, where eye movement trajectory data removes potential sources of error in image-based diagnostics.

Eye trackers collect eye movement trajectory data by emitting infrared light into the eyes of the viewer and capturing its reflection from the cornea, which is the transparent front part of the eye covering the pupil. Then the point of gaze is estimated from the relative positions of the pupil and the corneal reflection. In its most basic form, eye tracker data is a time series of the x and y coordinates of the eye movement trajectory in pixels relative to the screen resolution. Depending on the tracker model and the design of the experiment, there can be additional information such as the pupil diameter and a vector of the eye movement trajectory direction.

In this work we investigated different topological features extracted from human eye movement trajectories and compared them with specific macro-event statistics while solving a classification problem.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Eye movement trajectories have been investigated and measured since the beginning of the twentieth century [1]. Since then, they have had a long history of use in many areas of psychology, cognitive science and applied research fields [2]. During this long scientific history, the number of methods for quantitative characterization of eye movement trajectories did not change as dramatically as the number of scientific works using eye tracking methodology. Most quantitative measures take the form of macro-event statistics, where each eye movement trajectory is decomposed into saccades and fixations. Finding saccades in eye tracker data is strongly associated with velocity calculation, usually with a very simple two-point central difference approach [3]. The simple sample-to-sample difference is the easiest way; however, it significantly increases the noise of the signal [4]. All of this means that descriptive statistics based on macro events depend on the chosen algorithm of velocity approximation and are, in most cases, extremely unstable to noise in the signal. Therefore, new properties that holistically describe the entire eye movement trajectory extract quantitative features from the entire trajectory. Because of their holistic nature, topological features persist under any kind of random noise in the signal.

Eye movement trajectories are controlled by a vast and distributed neural system; therefore, they are affected by mental and neurological disorders such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and Parkinson’s disease [5]. Investigating new features of eye movement trajectories thus has the potential to facilitate the diagnosis of mental and neurological disorders. Other plausible areas that could benefit from better features are ophthalmology [6] and medical decision-making, where eye movement trajectory data eliminates potential sources of error in image-based diagnostics [7].

Eye trackers collect eye movement trajectory data by emitting infrared light into the viewer’s eyes and capturing its reflection from the cornea, the transparent front part of the eye that covers the pupil. The point of gaze is then estimated from the relative positions of the pupil and the corneal reflection. In its most basic form, eye tracker data is a time series of the x and y coordinates of the eye movement trajectory in pixels relative to the screen resolution. Additional information, such as the pupil diameter and a vector of eye movement trajectory direction, can be included depending on the tracker model and the experiment design.

In this work, we have investigated different topological features extracted from human eye movement trajectories and compared them with specific macro-event statistics in solving a classification problem.

References:

[2] . Andrew T Duchowski. Eye tracking methodology: Theory and practice . Springer, 2017.
